turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Yeah, thanks. Um... well, I guess what finally pushed me to make the appointment is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts in my life anymore. Between my patent notes, prep for this workshop I'm doing, gallery deadlines, team decisions at work... it's just all piling up. 

Actually, the gallery thing is kind of a funny story. The curator is this guy I met at a coffee shop, and he has this amazing vintage espresso machine behind the counter. I spent like two hours talking to him last week about the boiler pressure on those old Italian models. I've always wanted to restore one myself, you know? Just take it completely apart on the workbench and clean all the copper fittings. My wife says I have enough half-finished projects in the garage, but... 

Sorry, what was I talking about? Right, the moving parts. I just can't keep them straight. I end up just starting whatever is loudest—like whoever is messaging me on Slack right that second—instead of what actually matters. So, yeah. That's why I'm here.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions having 'half-finished projects in the garage,' indicating a pattern of failing to finish tasks or activities.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they 'can't seem to organize all the moving parts' in their life and struggle to prioritize what actually matters.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by going off on a tangent about an espresso machine, losing their train of thought, and admitting they get easily distracted by extraneous stimuli like Slack messages.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back, did you experience similar trouble with organization or finishing what you started when you were a kid?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, definitely. Even way back in grade school, actually. My parents used to dread parent-teacher conferences because my teachers would always write the exact same thing on my report cards—that I was a bright kid, but I just daydreamed all day. 

Which, to be fair, my third-grade classroom looked right out over the playground, and they were building this massive new wooden jungle gym that year. You know the kind with the huge tire swings and the rope bridges? You never really see those anymore because of the safety regulations, which I totally get, but the new plastic ones just don't have the same structural integrity. I actually read this really fascinating article a while back about how modern playground design is negatively impacting spatial awareness in kids, and... 

Um, wait. Sorry. What was the question? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, the organization was terrible. I would literally finish my assignments at home and then just forget to turn them in. Or I'd completely lose my homework folders. This was all long before I was even a teenager. It's just always been like this.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to follow through on schoolwork by forgetting to turn in completed assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly confirms that their organization was terrible during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports a history of completely losing necessary items, such as homework folders.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes daydreaming in class and demonstrates distractibility during the interview by going on a tangent and forgetting the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel physically restless, like you have a hard time sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, not really in a hyper way, I guess? But... yeah, actually. Especially when I'm stuck on these long design calls at work. I just feel this weird pressure building up in my chest and my legs, like I physically need to move. 

I actually ended up buying this standing desk a few months ago hoping it would help. It's one of those motorized ones with the dual motors. I spent like three weeks researching the weight capacity and the decibel rating of the lift mechanism because some of the cheaper ones sound like a dying lawnmower when you adjust them. I even looked into building my own out of extruded aluminum framing, which is actually super versatile stuff. You can build almost anything with 80/20 aluminum—3D printer frames, custom shelving... 

Anyway, the desk didn't really fix it. Even when I'm trying to look totally focused on the webcam, I'm just shifting from chair to chair, or I end up turning the camera off so I can pace around my office. I just can't stay planted in one spot for that long.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes leaving their seat to pace around the office during long design calls when they are expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms feeling a physical pressure and need to move, describing an inability to stay planted in one spot.

turns.doctor_question: Do these challenges with focus, restlessness, and starting projects come and go in distinct phases, or have they been fairly constant throughout your life?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I wouldn't say they come and go. It's more like they've just... always been there, humming in the background. It's just a constant thing for me. Like, there was never a time where I suddenly felt totally put together and then lost it again. It's just always been a mess. 

Actually, speaking of a mess, my garage is a total disaster right now. I was trying to organize my tool chests last weekend, and I bought these foam inserts where you trace all your wrenches and cut out the shapes so everything has a specific spot. It's brilliant in theory. Aviation mechanics use a system like that so they don't accidentally leave a socket wrench inside a jet engine, which, obviously, would be catastrophic. The amount of engineering that goes into those turbine blades is incredible, they have to withstand insane temperatures and centrifugal forces... 

But yeah, I got halfway through cutting out the foam for my metric wrenches, got distracted by an old carburetor I needed to rebuild, and now there are just little foam bits all over the floor. So, no, it's not phases. It's just... every day. Always.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes starting a project to cut out foam inserts for tools but failing to finish it.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient notes their garage is a 'total disaster' and describes ongoing struggles with organizing their tool chests.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they 'got distracted by an old carburetor' while working, and their speech demonstrates distractibility by going on a tangent about aviation mechanics.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself interrupting other people or finishing their sentences before they are done speaking?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I don't think I do that. If anything, I'm usually the one who trails off and forgets what I was saying halfway through a sentence. But interrupting? No, I usually just sit back and let people talk. 

Actually, speaking of people talking, my neighbor Dave—he's the one who's always working on his landscaping—he can talk for literally hours without taking a breath. He came over while I was trying to fix my sprinkler system last week. Which, by the way, those PVC pipes are a nightmare if you don't use the right primer before the cement. I ended up having to dig up a whole section of the lawn because the pressure blew out a joint I didn't set right. It's crazy how much water pressure those municipal lines have. You'd think they'd regulate it more at the street level, but they just rely on the pressure reducing valve at the house... 

Anyway, Dave came over and just started talking about his new riding mower, and I don't think I got a single word in for twenty minutes. So, no, I definitely don't interrupt people. I kind of wish I did sometimes, just to escape Dave.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient admits to trailing off and forgetting what they were saying mid-sentence, and demonstrates distractibility by going on a long tangent about their neighbor and sprinkler system.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient states they 'usually just sit back and let people talk,' denying that they talk excessively.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient denies the doctor's question about finishing other people's sentences.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting others, stating 'But interrupting? No.'
